On Dharma (End of Part 8). Regarding the reason why this chapter appears, there are generally three meanings.

First, it clarifies the universal practice of contemplation (*guanxing*). [The preceding... *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly with "前" (preceding), indicating the fragmentary nature of the input.*
Having contemplated the emptiness of karma, one now contemplates the emptiness of dharmas.
These two [contemplations] arise for the purpose of destroying afflictions.
From the first chapter up to the contemplation of karma refers to the specific destruction of [afflictions] within the dharmas.
This is analytical contemplation (*vibhāga-vipaśyanā*).
Now, if one contemplates both persons and phenomena collectively, designating them all as "dharmas," this is called collective contemplation (*saṃgraha-vipaśyanā*).
Therefore, the treatise refutes the four conditions through both general and specific analyses.
The Sūtra elucidates the teaching of the two aspects: the detailed and the concise.
Question: Is it the case that the method for refuting inverted phenomena is called the "contemplation of phenomena"?
To contemplate the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is what is meant by "dharma.
The answer is that both terms possess two meanings.
First, because one seeks and finds no such thing as a phenomenon of inversion, it is called "contemplating dharma" (*dharmānupaśyanā*).
Second, one contemplates that whether persons or phenomena, their myriad transformations are all different, yet they are all the dharma of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
This causes those who seek the principle to thereby attain awakening and entry.
Thus, the text says:
"If all phenomena are ultimately empty and this is their true nature (*dharmatā*), how does one enter it?
This is the core intent [of the question].
The question asks: This treatise refutes all false, biased, and deviant views to reveal the true path and the true nature.
Why is it that they are not explained at the very beginning,
rather than being clarified only at the end while being discussed in the middle?
The answer is that there are briefly two reasons.
First, regarding the sequence of refutation and exposition:
when heterodox teachings obscure the orthodox scriptures, their meaning is not clearly illuminated;
it is necessary to refute the heterodox so that the sublime essence may become manifest.
Therefore, it is only upon reaching this chapter that [the teaching] can finally be expounded.
Furthermore, this treatise, consisting of twenty-five chapters, broadly unfolds three main intentions.
The first seventeen chapters refute and cleanse [misconceptions regarding] the person and phenomena to clarify the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Now, this chapter clarifies the attainment of benefits.
Following the "Chapter on Destroying Time," it further refutes attachments to once again elucidate the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Question: For what reason is this section composed?
Answer: Based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, I shall explain the "Chapter on Practice and Response.
First, it describes the bodhisattva’s practice and response to *prajñā*;
next, in the middle section, it clarifies the attainment of benefits.
That is to say: the extinction of grave offenses, the protection by all devas, and the completion of the attainment of benefits;
having clarified what should be practiced, the Tathāgata has spoken these three aspects in this sutra.
The meaning of the Bodhisattva’s composition of this treatise is likewise so.
From the beginning up to this point, he has refuted the heterodox and revealed the orthodox;
yet those who hear it do not know what benefit is gained through such refutation and revelation.
Therefore, this chapter clarifies the attainment of benefits.
Although the attainment of benefits has been concluded, doubts and attachments have not yet been exhausted;
thus, false views are further refuted to once again clarify the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, having already heard [the teaching] and gained benefit, one then delights in hearing it again;
though one has previously gained benefit, one subsequently advances toward deeper realization.
Moreover, although one gains benefit later on, one attains the non-attainment of anything.
Therefore, he once again refutes the heterodox to reveal the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Of these three [sections], from the preceding parts onward the essence of the true mark has been clarified;
this present chapter clarifies the function of the true mark.
Question: What is the essence of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), and what is its function?
Answer: All ninety-six schools of heterodox practitioners say: [as follows].
"In the world there is only I alone; in the world there is only my one Way.
Each claims his own dharma is real while all others are false."
The Abhidharmikas designate the principle of the Four Noble Truths as "reality.
The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Only the principle of emptiness and equality within the single Truth of Cessation is called reality."
In the southern lands, the Mahāyāna refers to the principle of the destruction of the [four] truths as reality.
In the northern regions, the *prajñāpāramitā* of *bhūtalakṣaṇa* (the true mark) is termed reality.

Furthermore, among the scholars of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the principles of the two kinds of selflessness, the three natures of non-existence, and the *amala-vijñāna* are called reality, while all else is deemed illusory.
Now, examining this in its entirety:
if there were a principle called "the view of eternalism," it would be false and not real.
If there were not even a single principle, it would likewise be a false view and a delusion,
rather than being true.
To claim both existence and non-existence is to fully embrace the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
To say "neither existent nor non-existent" is the discourse of the deluded.
If one is fully possessed of the four positions, then all manner of views arise;
if there are no four positions at all, that constitutes a great annihilationism.
Now, it is clear that if one can be free from these conceptualizations so that the mind has nothing upon which to rely,
I do not know how to name it; I shall tentatively call it the "true nature" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the root of both delusion and awakening.
To awaken to it, there are the worthies and sages of the three vehicles.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
There are three types of those who perceive the Middle Way:
because they observe with inferior wisdom, they attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
because they observe with middling wisdom, they attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
Because those of superior wisdom contemplate it, they attain unsurpassed bodhi;
yet, by being deluded regarding this true reality (*dharmatā*), there arises the chaotic cycle of birth and death within the six realms.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
All phenomena are established based on the root of non-abiding;
yet the essence of the true mark contains all virtues and does not exist outside of the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Exhausting all skillful means and encompassing every gateway,
I shall now briefly cite two of them.
First, clarifying essence and function in relation to persons;
second, clarifying essence and function in relation to dharmas.
Regarding the clarification of essence and function in relation to persons:
The following verse states:
"Within the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, there is neither self nor non-self.
This clarifies the essence of true reality with respect to persons.
The Buddhas have sometimes spoken of a self and sometimes of non-self.
Since the essence and function of self and non-self are thus, whether it be the permanent or the impermanent,

the ultimate or the conventional, the three vehicles or the one vehicle, the five schools or the eighteen schools, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the more than thirty disputes, or even the five hundred schools and the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates— all are the functioning of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
These are reconciled through four perspectives without contradiction:
first, they are taught in accordance with the world;
second, they are taught as antidotes.
Third, each [teaching] is explained for the sake of specific individuals;
fourth, it is explained by way of the gate of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, one who studies this treatise thoroughly awakens to all the Buddha’s teachings.
Second, regarding the elucidation of essence and function through the Dharma:
the following verse states that "all things are real, unreal, both real and unreal, and neither real nor unreal.
These four gates are all skillful means for the true mark (*dharmatā*).
By allowing the mind to roam through the four gates, one enters the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
Therefore, the four gates function as the means, while non-fourness constitutes the essence.
This shall be fully explained later.
It arises proximately from the preceding chapter on Karma.

In that previous chapter, it was established through the profound transformation of heavy matters that the causes and effects of human phenomena are ultimately empty; this is precisely the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
An opponent says:
If that is so, how can one enter?
To answer this question now:
before entering the true nature of reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa), you must first wash away the views regarding both the subject who enters and the object entered; only then can entry be attained.
Therefore, this chapter has come forth.
Question: What is the meaning of "dharma"?
Answer: To speak according to principle:
It is simply the True Dharma (saddharma).
As it is said: "The nature of the True Dharma is detachment," and so forth;
and again: [it is said].
"All those who are unimpeded, through the single path, transcend birth and death," and so forth.
If categorized according to their functional meaning, there are three kinds of *dharma*:
first, that which serves as a norm is called *dharma*.
This refers to the Buddha’s principles and teachings.
Second, "Dharma" refers to its own essence;
this term can also apply generally to both principles and teachings.
This refers to form, mind, and so forth.
Third, that which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of the mental consciousness is termed "dharmas.
This is stated with reference to the objective sphere.
That which is the object of the eye is form (*rūpa*);
likewise, up to that which is the object of the body is called tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*).
Now, because this is the object of the mind (*manas*), it is called phenomena (*dharma*).
The *dharmadhātu* is so named because it serves as the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), encompassing all seventeen realms mentioned above.
The eighteenth chapter of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies the objects of consciousness and the objects of wisdom.
The various non-Buddhists also possess these three factors;
however, the non-Buddhists further maintain a distinct category of objects of consciousness known as "divine" (īśvara).
The Sāṃkhya school likewise elucidates these same three factors.
It is simply that there is no separate dharma as an object for a deity.
The *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"At that time, having transcended the realm of mind, one abides within the activity of wisdom."
Therefore, one should know that all objects of inverted perception are illusory transformations and cannot be found.
A question is raised:
The *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states, "One should eliminate only the illness, but not eliminate the dharma."
Why is this chapter titled "Refuting Dharmas"?
The answer is that there are two ways in which one does not eliminate those dharmas.
First, one perceives dharmas because of a spiritual affliction (*vyādhi*).
It is just as one with an eye disease sees flowers in the sky;
since there is no dharma that can be removed, it is said that "one does not remove its dharma.
What is now called "destroying dharmas" refers merely to destroying those diseased dharmas.
Second, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"One merely severs attachment to grasping, but does not sever the view of self.
This 'view of self' is precisely the Buddha-nature."
It is the same now as well:
one merely destroys the mind of grasping held by outsiders,
yet does not destroy the true nature of all phenomena.
Therefore, it simply says "contemplating the dharmas.
This chapter consists of three parts:
first, the introduction in prose.
The two verses primarily clarify the method of contemplation,
while the three prose sections provide an explanation.
The first section contains two questions and answers.
The intent of the previous question was as follows:
From the "Chapter on Causes and Conditions" through the "Chapter on Contemplating Karma," it is clarified that all phenomena are ultimately empty;
this is what is called the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
This summarizes what the Master of the Treatise has stated above.
To examine the intent of this summary: the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is designated as "Dharma.
Because one now contemplates this Dharma, it is called the "Chapter on the Contemplation of Dharmas" (*Dharmavipaśyanā-varga*).
What is meant by "entering"?
Entering is awakening; it is realization.
Therefore, one asks about entering.
However, the false and illusory cannot enter into the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, the true nature of reality cannot, in turn, enter into the true nature of reality.
Moreover, when one seeks the false and illusory, it cannot be found.
What thing could be brought into the true nature (bhūtalakṣaṇa)?
If one were to bring the true nature into the true nature,
then one would have to establish a limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi).
In reality, however, it is not so.
Regarding these two gateways, how does one enter?
The answer is: that which is called "entering" consists in the extinguishing of the notions of "I" and "mine."
The external intention says:
true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is that which is entered,
and the practitioner is the one who enters.
Nowadays, those who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna all say that there is someone capable of realizing bodhi;
thus, bodhi is that which is realized.
The Master of the Treatise says:
"If one can eliminate both the person who enters and the dharma that is entered, such that ultimately there is neither an enterer nor an entry, this is truly called 'entry.
As the *Avataṃsaka* says:
The profound realm of the Tathāgata is equal in measure to empty space;
all sentient beings enter into reality, yet there is nothing entered.
As the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* says:
The entry that is non-entry is called the entry into the Dharma.
It is also like when Śāriputra questioned the founder of the Prajñāpāramitā school:
"How does a bodhisattva practice prajñā?"
The Buddha, though not seeing it with his five eyes,
nevertheless rebuked him, saying:
"If you can remain unseen while practicing the essence of a bodhisattva, then you may proceed."
One does not perceive the word "bodhisattva," one does not perceive prajñā,
and one does not perceive practice.
"Not seeing and not practicing" is what is called a bodhisattva practicing *prajñā*.
Now, in the first fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the verse of Mākandika says:
It is not seen, heard, sensed, or known;
it is not obtained through the observance of precepts,
nor is it that which is not seen or heard.
It is not attained without maintaining the precepts.
An objection is raised:
"If that were so, one would attain the Way by practicing the 'dumb method'."
The Buddha replied:
"If you do not perceive all phenomena,
then at that time you would simply be mute."
This is also the intended meaning of the current text.
Question: Since the preceding section has already refuted the self (*ātman*), for what reason is it refuted again?
Answer: My illness is difficult to eliminate;
furthermore, it is the root of all delusions.
For this reason, I have repeatedly refuted it.
Furthermore, while the preceding sections have extensively refuted the doctrine of a substantial self,
this section correctly elucidates the entry into the contemplation of true reality (*tattvārtha*) to eliminate the subtle, nominal self.
If one says there is a person of the Mahāyāna named a "bodhisattva," [it is merely a designation].
If one wishes to practice the contemplation of the true nature (*dharmatā*),
it is immediately the view of "self" and "what belongs to self"; therefore,
it differs from the aforementioned [state].
The subsequent questions and answers follow the text as written.
The original verses within the "Guan" (Guangling) edition are divided into three parts;
the first five verses clarify how the śrāvakas receive the teaching and obtain benefit.
The next six verses clarify the benefits gained by bodhisattvas who receive the teaching;
the final verse clarifies the benefits gained by pratyekabuddhas.
The reason for specifically clarifying the śrāvakas first, followed by the bodhisattvas, is as follows:
Since these two alike received the Buddha’s teachings, they are explained together as one category;
because the pratyekabuddhas appear in a world where no Buddha exists and thus do not receive the Buddha’s teachings, they are discussed separately later on.
Just as there is a Śrāvaka-piṭaka and a Bodhisattva-piṭaka, but no Pratyekabuddha-piṭaka,
because Pratyekabuddhas do not receive formal instruction.
The first two chapters clarify the two Piṭakas;
they also represent the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, as well as the Half-Teaching and Full-Teaching.
Thus, they fully expound all the teachings.
By receiving these two teachings, one gains benefit;
this clarifies that all benefits are comprehensive.
It does not clarify the teachings for humans and devas.
If one clarifies the supramundane, then one fully attains the mundane.
Question: Since this is a Mahāyāna treatise, it should only clarify the benefits gained by bodhisattvas.
How is it that the teachings of the two vehicles and their benefits are clarified?
The answer is: this treatise demonstrates that there is nothing confused, nothing unrefuted, no teaching not proclaimed, and no benefit not fully provided;
only then is it truly Mahāyāna.
This is because the large encompasses the small.
The reason for presenting the small first and the large afterward is to demonstrate the sequence of the teachings and their benefits.
Furthermore, it is intended to show that the small is a provisional means (*upāya*) while the great is the ultimate reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
This indicates that the former opens the gate of provisional means, while the latter reveals the aspect of ultimate reality.
A person of recent times has said:
This was the division made by Master Yao of the Northern Land;
it is likely due to his failure to consult ancient commentaries that such an error occurred.
Furthermore, according to the end of the prose section:
This text was composed by Qingmu himself;
it is suitable for lecturers to employ.
One master, following the lineage of transmission, divided it into five parts.
The first one and a half lines clarify what is to be abandoned;
the next one and a half lines clarify the attainment of the wisdom of selflessness;
and the third two lines clarify the two types of nirvāṇa.
The fourth section, spanning five lines, provides a broad exposition of Buddhism;
the fifth section, spanning two lines, clarifies the benefits obtained by those of the three vehicles.
To explain this now would disrupt the order of the text.
One should employ the aforementioned intention.
Within the five verses, the contemplation of the śrāvakas is elucidated through two distinct sections.
The first one and a half verses provide an introduction to the teaching for śrāvakas.
The second section, consisting of three and a half verses, clarifies the benefits gained from receiving the teachings.
This section is further divided into two parts;
the first verse clarifies the teaching on the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
The subsequent half-verse clarifies the teaching on the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which likewise gives rise to the two kinds of emptiness: that of phenomena and that of persons.
This initial verse is further divided into two parts.
The first half refutes the self as being identical to the aggregates (*skandha*),
while the second half refutes the self as being separate from the aggregates.
The first half states:
Since the self is identical to the aggregates,
the self must likewise be subject to arising and ceasing.
If this were so, one would perceive only the five aggregates and not perceive a self.
Furthermore, if the self were the five aggregates, then since there are five aggregates, there would also have to be five selves; this would result in the loss of the singular self.
If one does not exist, then many cannot exist either.
This case should also be applied by analogy.
Since the self is identical to the aggregates,
if the self were one and an aggregate were also one, then the five aggregates would be lost.
Since the many do not exist, the one also does not exist.
However, at present, I am specifically refuting the self (*ātman*), not the aggregates (*skandha*).
Therefore, I merely [deny that] the self arises from the aggregates; I do not [assert that] the aggregates themselves are the self.
The latter half states:
"Since there is a self-substance apart from the aggregates,
there should likewise be a self-characteristic apart from the aggregates."
If one again takes the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) as the characteristic of the self (*ātman*),
then one should likewise take the substance of the aggregates as the substance of the self.
To conceive of a self in this way is the affliction of manifesting signs (*nimitta-kleśa*).
Furthermore, it says:
"I have four colors, such as red and white.
It also says: "I am like a pure pearl, a lamp, or a flame."
All [of these] take the characteristics of the aggregates as their characteristics;
therefore, we now challenge you:
you have not separately perceived a characteristic of a self that is distinct from the characteristics of the aggregates.
One should not take the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) as the characteristic of a self.
Question: Why do those who calculate a self take the characteristics of the aggregates as the characteristic of a self?
Answer: Because the aggregates encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Those who conceive of a self hear that the conditioned is used as a mark to prove the existence of a self;
since the unconditioned has no marks,
it cannot be cited as proof for a self.
If there is no self, the second [point] clarifies the non-self of phenomena (dharmanairātmya), which is also the emptiness of phenomena (dharmaśūnyatā).
Previously, one relied upon the aggregates (skandha) to eliminate the self; now, one relies upon the aggregates to eliminate phenomena.
This is borrowed from me to eliminate the aggregates (*skandha*).
Question: The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* clarifies that both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna possess the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Volume eighteen states:
The Master of the Treatise cites a Sūtra of the Hīnayāna, which says:
"What is old age and illness?
It is the emptiness of dharmas."
Who undergoes old age, sickness, and death?
It is said that persons are empty;
however, the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, and other texts clarify that the Hīnayāna realizes only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
How are they reconciled?
The answer is: in the Hīnayāna there are two types, the first being those of dull faculties and the second those of sharp faculties.
Those of sharp faculties fully attain both types of emptiness,
whereas those of dull faculties attain only the emptiness of persons;
these refer to the Abhidharma and the Satyasiddhi-śāstra respectively.
The Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) predominantly clarifies the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) and only rarely explains the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā),
whereas the Greater Vehicle (Mahāyāna) predominantly explains the emptiness of phenomena and only rarely clarifies the emptiness of persons.
In this discussion, we follow the majority rather than the minority.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra* clarifies only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Third, the Hīnayāna attains the full realization of the emptiness of persons;
because they all know that there is ultimately no self, it is said that they have attained the emptiness of persons.
They attain the emptiness of phenomena but do not exhaust it;
they do not know that the intrinsic nature of phenomena is empty,
nor do they know that all phenomena within and without the triple world are empty.
Therefore, for this reason, the emptiness of the Śrāvaka-dharma is not taught.
Because it eliminates the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," the second section below clarifies the benefits gained from receiving the teaching; this further has two parts.
The first clarifies the benefit of attaining the wisdom of the two kinds of non-self.
Next, one obtains the two benefits of nirvāṇa:
the former is the benefit of the cause, and the latter is the benefit of the fruit;
the former is the benefit of wisdom, and the latter is the benefit of abandonment.
The former is the attainment of the Path, and the latter is the realization of Cessation.
Furthermore, the former consists of conditioned merits, while the latter consists of unconditioned merits;
these are also the two liberations: the conditioned and the unconditioned.
The essential points of the Śrāvaka school do not exceed these two.
The first [of these] further consists of two parts;
the first correctly explains the attainment of the wisdom of selflessness.
Next is the praise of the Dharma and its recipients.
The first part follows the text as it stands.
From "Having attained the wisdom of non-self" onwards is the second chapter, the praise of the Dharma and its recipients.
The first half praises the Dharma, while the second half praises the beautiful woman.
Regarding "internal and external self and what belongs to the self," the second section clarifies the attainment of the two fruits of *nirvāṇa*.
Because one cultivates the causal wisdom of the two kinds of non-self (*anātman*), one attains the two fruits of *nirvāṇa*.
This is, in essence, the primary tenet of the Śrāvaka meaning.
Taken according to the text, there are two parts.
The first verse clarifies the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder).
The following verse clarifies the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
In terms of the sequence of practice,
one first attains the state with remainder, and subsequently attains the state without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).

Regarding the fact that the preceding section clarifies the state without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*) while the subsequent section clarifies the state with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa*), there are generally two meanings.
First, the present [section] is a pedagogical method (*deśanāmukha*);
it first explains the commonality and profundity [of these states] to inspire longing and the pursuit of them.

Second, as the interlocking structure of the textual sequence clearly demonstrates, because one extinguishes the self and what belongs to the self (*ātman-ātmīya*), one immediately attains the state of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
The first half of the verse restates the preceding [point].
Regarding "the internal and external self and what belongs to the self":
I am that which is internal;
that for the sake of which [the body] exists is external.
Furthermore, within the aggregates (skandhas), I am the internal.
The self that is separate from the aggregates is external.
Its objects are also of two kinds:
the five aggregates are internal objects.
The jar and the cloth constitute the external objects;
the various sensations constitute cessation.
"I" and "mine" are the afflictions of view.
Feeling is the latent tendency of attachment and craving; furthermore,
the former pertains to the vision of the truths,
while the latter pertains to reflection.
Because all views are extinguished, all sensations are extinguished.
Because craving and views are extinguished, the retributive body is extinguished.
In the former case, because views are extinguished, craving is extinguished.
With the cessation of sensation, the body ceases;
this is the cessation of the effect due to the cessation of the cause.
Because karma and afflictions have ceased, the second [type of] nirvāṇa with remainder is clarified.
The first half of the verse clearly elucidates the cessation of karmic activity;
the second half explains the reason for this cessation.
Since karma and afflictions are illusory and unreal, upon awakening to ultimate emptiness, all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is extinguished.

Question: How many kinds of "remainder" and "remainderlessness" are there? Answer: Briefly, there are three kinds: first, the remainder and remainderlessness of the Hīnayāna; second, the remainder and remainderlessness of the Mahāyāna; and third, the remainder and remainderlessness of the ultimate reality (dharmatā). Regarding the first, the remainder and remainderlessness of the Hīnayāna: there are two types of remainder and remainderlessness for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. What are these two? First, the remainder of the aggregates (*skandha-śeṣa*); second, the remainderlessness of the aggregates (*skandha-niḥśeṣa*). What is meant by the remainder of the aggregates? It refers to the state where the afflictions have been exhausted but the life-force has not yet ended. What is meant by the remainderlessness of the aggregates? It refers to the state where both the afflictions and the life-force have been exhausted. Furthermore, there are two types of remainder and remainderlessness for bodhisattvas. What are these two? First, the remainder of the afflictions (*kleśa-śeṣa*); second, the remainderlessness of the afflictions (*kleśa-niḥśeṣa*). What is meant by the remainder of the afflictions? It refers to the state where the afflictions have been exhausted but the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been eliminated. What is meant by the remainderlessness of the afflictions? It refers to the state where both the afflictions and the habitual tendencies have been exhausted. This is called the remainder and remainderlessness of the Hīnayāna. As for the remainder and remainderlessness of the Mahāyāna: what is meant by the remainder of the Mahāyāna? It refers to the state where the afflictions have been exhausted but the habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated. What is meant by the remainderlessness of the Mahāyāna? It refers to the state where both the afflictions and the habitual tendencies have been exhausted. This is called the remainder and remainderlessness of the Mahāyāna. As for the remainder and remainderlessness of the ultimate reality: what is meant by the remainder of the ultimate reality? It refers to the state where the afflictions have been exhausted but the habitual tendencies have not yet been eliminated. What is meant by the remainderlessness of the ultimate reality? It refers to the state where both the afflictions and the habitual tendencies have been exhausted. This is called the remainder and remainderlessness of the ultimate reality. Second, the remainder and non-remainder of the Mahāyāna;

Regarding the remainder and non-remainder of the Hīnayāna:
One explanation states:
the exhaustion of the fetters of the [defiled] aggregates is called "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa), because there still remains a residual burden; therefore, it is named "with remainder."
Master Zhaolun said:
"Because residual traces have not yet vanished and residual conditions have not yet been exhausted, it is called 'with remainder' (sopadhiśeṣa).
If the retribution body is eliminated and no further burdens remain, it is called 'without remainder' (nirupadhiśeṣa)."
Next it says:
Because the severing of the fetters of the "son" (the individual) has been completed, yet the attainment of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not yet sufficient,
that which remains of the unconditioned is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*).
If the unconditioned *saṃbhogakāya* were extinguished, that would suffice; therefore, it is called "without remainder.
Regarding the Mahāyāna distinction between "with remainder" and "without remainder":
the extinction of the afflictions of the five stages is termed "with remainder."
The extinction of the retribution of death is termed "without remainder.
However, while the two types of nirvana are attained sequentially in the Hīnayāna,
they are attained simultaneously in the Mahāyāna.
When the delusions of the five stages are exhausted, the two types of death collapse.
Furthermore, in the Hīnayāna, one first attains the state with remainder and subsequently attains the state without remainder;
in the Mahāyāna, one first attains the state without remainder, which is the Dharmakāya.
The two bodies—the *nirmāṇakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*—which arise subsequently, are termed "with remainder.
Furthermore, according to the Mahāyāna, three types of nirvāṇa are distinguished based on the three bodies:
the *dharmakāya* is the nirvāṇa without remainder.
The two bodies—the transformation body and the enjoyment body—are called nirvana with remainder.
Taken together with the third body, they constitute non-abiding nirvana;
for by means of the dharma-body, one does not abide in saṃsāra.
The two bodies—the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*)—do not abide in nirvāṇa.
Because both have extinguished attachment to the two extremes, they are called "nirvāṇa without abiding.
This passage appears in the "Chapter on the Three Bodies" of the seven-fascicle *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* elucidates four types of nirvāṇa.
Three are as described above;
next, it clarifies that intrinsic purity (*prakṛtiviśuddhi*) is termed nirvāṇa.
Regarding the combined discussion of the Great and Small Vehicles concerning the "with remainder" and "without remainder":
in the Small Vehicle, both "with remainder" and "without remainder" are considered to be with remainder;
in the Great Vehicle, both "with remainder" and "without remainder" are termed without remainder.
This is the intent of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Regarding the second section, which clarifies the bodhisattva’s contemplation following the Buddhas’ discourse on the "self":
why is it that the contemplation of the śrāvaka is explained first, followed by the clarification of the bodhisattva’s contemplation?
Answer: It is because one wishes to clarify the progression from the shallow to the profound that the small comes first and the great later;
furthermore, it is because one wishes to lead those of the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle that the small precedes the great.
Question: In what way do the contemplations of the Small and Great Vehicles differ?
Answer: The insight of the śrāvakas is shallow;
they take "self" as a provisional means and "non-self" as the ultimate truth.
Here, it is clarified that both "self" and "non-self" are merely provisional means.
That neither self nor non-self is [ultimately] real constitutes the profound contemplation of the Bodhisattva; thus,
they take both self and non-self as skillful means.
From the perspective of a śrāvaka, the śrāvaka path is considered a skillful means;
from the perspective of a bodhisattva, it is regarded as the ultimate reality.
This corresponds to the textual passage in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*: "This alone is the one true reality; the other two are not real. Thus, the meaning of the texts converges.
If a follower of the Mahāyāna were to take the two selves as a skillful means and regard non-self as the ultimate reality,
this would still be the contemplation of a Śrāvaka.
Furthermore, because they originally attained the Great [Vehicle], the Small [Vehicle] is thereby established.
Since neither "great" can be attained nor "small" established, those who grasp at something to be attained and cling to the two kinds of selflessness merely produce false views.
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva, both "self" and "selflessness" are expedient means; it is that which is neither self nor selfless that is the reality.
Those who have attained realization hold that non-self is merely a skillful means;
since they do not attain the real, they likewise do not attain the provisional.
To speak of it in general terms:
Those who possess [limited] attainment cling to the two kinds of selflessness;
they do not encompass the Great and Small Vehicles, nor do they grasp at the provisional or the ultimate.
Since both "self" and "selflessness" are merely skillful means, [they are ultimately empty].

The skillful means of the three natures and the three absences of nature are not themselves the ultimate reality; rather, that which is neither the three natures nor the three absences of nature is the true reality.
This principle applies to all things.
Question: How is it known that the former is the contemplation of the śrāvaka and the latter is the contemplation of the bodhisattva?
Answer: It is proven by the very words that distinguish between the shallow and the profound;
thus, it is known to be so.
Furthermore, because Śrāvakas cultivate the contemplation of non-self with the desire to seek the two fruits of Nirvāṇa,
this is merely the principle of self-deliverance.
The preceding section has correctly elucidated this teaching.
Therefore, it is known that this is the contemplation of the śrāvakas.
Now, this chapter extensively distinguishes how the bodhisattva transforms sentient beings through boundless means and possesses all gates of teaching;
thus, it is known that this is the contemplation of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, the prose section below, as explained by Qingmu (*Sengzhao*), cites the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* because the Bodhisattva contemplates it:
"The Bodhisattva neither practices with a self, nor does he practice without a self.
This citation was indeed made by the prose section itself.
This is not a case of the commentator’s forced interpretation;
rather, it is divided into two parts according to the text.
First, three verses clarify the phenomena observed by the bodhisattva.
The second three verses clarify the characteristics of those who benefit from the Bodhisattva [teachings].
In the aforementioned Śrāvaka Dharma, these two chapters were also established:
first, the teaching on the non-self of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), followed by the teaching on the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
This refers to the dual teaching.
Later, wisdom and severance are clarified as the two benefits.
Now, within the Mahāyāna as well, the two teachings are first elucidated, followed by the discernment of the dual benefits.
The three verses constitute two sections.
The first verse sets forth the two topical headings of skillful means and the true nature (*dharmatā*).
The second section consists of two verses that explain these two topical headings.
The first half of the verse indicates the section on skillful means (*upāya*), while the second half indicates the section on ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Question: For what reason is the skillful means regarding self and non-self explained first?
Answer: To respond directly to the Śrāvakas, "self" is taught as a skillful means (*upāya*), while "non-self" is the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
This is like the principle of emptiness and non-self within the sixteen truths of the Abhidharma;
it is also as stated by the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*: [text follows].
In the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) there is a self, while in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) there is no self.
Therefore, it is now clarified that for a bodhisattva, whether [the śrāvaka] perceives a self or no-self is entirely a skillful means (*upāya*).
This is why the initial exposition distinguishes between the skillful means of self and no-self.
Since both "self" and "non-self" are skillful means,
the same applies by analogy to "permanent" and "impermanent.
Therefore, what was previously taught as "impermanence" is likewise a skillful means.
The present teaching that [the Buddha] is eternal and blissful is also a skillful means (*upāya*).
In this manner, all meanings of the three vehicles and the one vehicle are analogous.
The second half of the verse clarifies the gateway to the ultimate reality (*tattva*).
That is to say: it is neither self nor non-self, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither three nor one; all such meanings are of this same category.
The first half [of the verse] pertains to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the second half pertains to ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The first half constitutes the three *siddhāntas*, while the second half is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Furthermore, the first half may also be understood as the two truths: the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the ultimate (*satya*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*), persons and so forth exist;
from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), they do not exist."
Thus we know that taking "self" as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and "non-self" as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)—
whereas the latter half, which is neither self nor non-self— is the Middle Way, the single true reality (*eka-satya*). Furthermore,
the former half is called the "half-character" (*ardha-akṣara*) teaching.
The ultimate completion of the lower half constitutes the "full letter" (pūrṇākṣara).
However, if one discusses that which is fully complete,
both the upper and lower halves are merely "half-letters" (ardhakṣara).
When neither-self, selflessness, and the selflessness of the self are fully possessed, it is called "complete" (pūrṇa-akṣara).
Furthermore, the first half [of the verse] constitutes the gate of teaching (upadeśa),
while the second half is termed the principle (tattva).
The meaning of these verses is richly multivalent and cannot be fully exhausted by a single approach.
Regarding the "true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena," the following second section consists of two verses that explain the topical headings (*uddāna*).
The first verse provides an immediate explanation of the heading concerning true reality.
The second verse explains the topical section on skillful means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, since it was previously clarified that one enters the true nature (*dharmatā*) by means of skillful means,
skillful means is explained first and the true nature is subsequently analyzed.
Now, arising from the true nature (*dharmatā*) through skillful means (*upāya*),
the true nature is presented first and the skillful means follow.
"The true nature of all phenomena" reiterates the section on the true nature from the second half of the preceding verse.
The phrase "the activities of mind and speech are severed" explains the meaning of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
First, the true mark is explained by way of the teaching of phenomena (*dharmadeśanā*):
because it vertically transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the mind of the four propositions perishes.
Because one has horizontally transcended the hundred negations, the mind of the hundred negations is severed.
As it is with the mind,
so it is with speech.
The words of the four propositions cannot express it;
the discourse of the hundred negations cannot describe it.
Furthermore, it is not merely that the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is ineffable.
Since even speech is itself the true nature (*dharmatā*), although there is speech, it is non-speech.
Therefore, the goddess challenged Śāriputra, saying:
"You merely know that the true nature is beyond words; you have not yet realized that words themselves are the true nature."
Therefore, it is said that while speech fills the ten directions, it is eternally characterized by these four absences.
Question: Why is this so?
Answer: If there is a substance of speech, it is inherently existent from the very beginning.
This is termed "permanence.
Permanence cannot be expressed in words;
now, because of causes and conditions, every word spoken lacks intrinsic nature.
Therefore, there are no words;
for although one speaks, it is because from the very beginning there has been no speaking.
As the *Karmavibhaṅga* states:
All karmas are fundamentally unarisen,
because they lack a fixed nature;
likewise, one should say that all words are fundamentally without words.
This is because they lack a fixed nature.
As it is with words,
so it is with mental activities.
First, the true mark transcends the four propositions, such that the mind cannot take them as an object.
Second, the very object of cognition is itself the true mark;
thus, although it universally takes all phenomena as objects, it remains eternally beyond the four propositions.
Regarding the phrase "neither arising nor ceasing," the second half of the verse is explained by way of analogy:
because the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) are unable to produce it, it is called "non-arising."
Because it cannot be extinguished even by forceful suppression, it is called "non-extinction.
Furthermore, the previous statement regarding the extinction of the mind clarifies that,
according to the fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*), [dharmas] are fundamentally unarisen and likewise non-extinguished now.
It is not that there are four propositions regarding the arising of speech and its subsequent cessation.
Since this is so for speech,
it is likewise so for the mind.
Regarding "quiescent and extinguished like nirvāṇa":
those who are deluded all claim that within saṃsāra there is arising and ceasing, whereas in nirvāṇa there is no arising or ceasing.
Therefore, one borrows the metaphor of nirvāṇa to illustrate saṃsāra.
What you call birth-and-death is like your own nirvāṇa;
therefore it is said that "quiescent extinction is like nirvāṇa.

This now clarifies that the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is not the same as the principle of the True Dharma (satyadharma) of the South, nor the Prajñā-pāramitā of the Real Mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) of the North.
Furthermore, it differs from the *Purāṇa-ṭīkā*’s ālayavijñāna, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*’s late [interpretation], and the Mahāyāna amala-vijñāna;
these all likewise share the Vātsīputrīya’s conception of a self (ātman), and thus there remains a rational basis for its existence.
Now we shall discuss only that form is the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Just as a conventional designation of form can neither be said to exist nor to not exist,
one cannot find form when seeking it through the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*).
Therefore, form (*rūpa*) is itself the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, fascicle 42, explains:
"What is the mark of form?"
What is the characteristic of consciousness?
Non-existence is the characteristic of form;
non-existence is the characteristic of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Furthermore, the Lord of Devas praised Subhūti’s discourse,
noting that he expounded the true nature of phenomena without destroying conventional designations.
Thus, one knows that conventional designations are vividly present and are themselves the true nature of phenomena.
Regarding "All things are both real and unreal," this is the second explanation of the preceding section on the preliminary means (*upāya*).
Question: Previously, the self (*ātman*) and non-self (*anātman*) were used as the preliminary means;
why is it now explained by means of the real and the unreal?
Furthermore, previously, the two pairs of "self" and "non-self" were treated as skillful means (*upāya*),
while "neither self nor non-self" was taken as the reality.
Why is it now that the fourfold tetralemma of the real and the unreal is used to explain the aforementioned skillful means?
I replied: "I have listened to this for many years and lectured upon it for a long time,
yet I have never seen a scriptural passage or a commentary that explains this meaning."
Now, to briefly clarify the function of consciousness for future sages:
the previous explanation that "self" and "non-self" serve as skillful means was intended as a skillful means for those of the Two Vehicles, wherein there is no self and no real self.
Therefore, it is clarified that whether provisional or ultimate, the two vehicles are both expedient means when compared to the bodhisattva;
rather, neither-self nor non-self constitutes the true reality.
Now, in this *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, that which is the true reality is as follows:
The preceding section clarified that the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena transcends mental activity and verbal expression;
this section clarifies that the true nature realized by the Bodhisattva is severed from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Although the true nature is severed from the words of the four propositions, [it remains ineffable].
One must rely on the words of the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) in order to attain awakening and entry into the true nature of reality (dharmatā). Therefore,
the transcendence of the four propositions is taken as the reality,
while the four propositions themselves are taken as the skillful means (upāya).
This interpretation truly accords with the intent of the scriptural text.
Question: For what reason are the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) taken as the skillful means, while the transcendence of the four propositions is taken as the ultimate truth?
Answer: It is because one wishes to encompass all principles and teachings exhaustively.
Now, regarding the discussion of teachings, they do not go beyond the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);
thus, the four propositions encompass all verbal teachings without exception.
Now, when discussing the ultimate principle, it culminates in the transcendence of the four [conditions].
Thus, by means of the transcendence of the four, the ultimate principle is clarified.
Although this constitutes but a single chapter of discourse, it comprehensively encompasses all the principles, teachings, and practices of the Buddha-dharma, such that they are complete.
Question: Why was "self" and "non-self" used as the skillful means previously, while now "real" and "unreal" are used as the skillful means?
Answer: It is because one wishes to demonstrate that the true nature (dharmatā) is the very essence, and that within this essence there is no duality whatsoever.
Therefore, having previously clarified the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa),
[the text] now reiterates the true mark in order to explain it.
It demonstrates that expedient means (upāya) are functional, and that these functions have many gateways.
Therefore, previously the skillful means of self and non-self were shown; now the skillful means of the real and the unreal are shown.
Question: Why was the skillful means of self and non-self employed above, while here the skillful means of the real and the unreal are clarified?
Answer: For the Śrāvakas above, I taught "self" as a provisional means and "non-self" as the reality;
I taught "dharmas" as a provisional means and "the absence of dharmas" as the ultimate truth.
For those above the Śrāvakas, I clarified that both "self" and "non-self" are merely provisional means, and that neither "self" nor "non-self" constitutes the ultimate reality.
Now, in contrast to the śrāvakas, the existence of dharmas and the non-existence of dharmas are both skillful means; neither dharma nor non-dharma constitutes the ultimate reality.
Therefore, it is now clarified what is real and what is unreal.
Regarding the text, there are two parts:
the first three phrases correctly clarify the skillful means,
while the fourth phrase summarizes the purport of the teaching.
Among these, the four propositions are taught for bodhisattvas of the three capacities.
The statement that "all is real and all is unreal" is for those of middling capacity;
this is analogous to the meaning of the Kaishan school.
Both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are worldly conventions and are false;
they are called unreal.
Entering the ultimate truth (paramārtha) means neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
This is called "real.
The second phrase is both real and unreal, as it transforms those of inferior faculties;
this is like the meaning of "ornamentation."
Because birth and death are illusory, they are unreal;
because nirvāṇa is not illusory, it is real.
The third—being neither real nor unreal—is for the sake of bodhisattvas of the highest faculties, clarifying that birth and death and nirvāṇa have never been real, nor have they ever been unreal.
This school represents the intent studied by the present-day Nāgārjuna.
Regarding the sequence for dispelling defects through the three statements,
those of inferior capacity say:
Birth-and-death is unreal, while nirvana is real.
Those of middling faculties say:
"This birth-and-death and nirvana are both entirely unreal."
Neither birth-and-death nor nirvana—this is the reality of all things.
Those of superior capacity say:
"It is not a 'neither birth-and-death-nor-nirvana' reality."
Nor is it that saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are unreal.
Furthermore, the first phrase represents the doctrine of the Ekavyāvahārika school;
because they maintain that both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are merely conventional designations, they are called "Ekavyāvahārika" (Those Who Propound a Single [Conventional] Teaching).
The second sentence represents the doctrine of the Lokottaravādins:
because the dharmas of birth and death in the mundane world arise from unreal causes,
they are called "real."
Furthermore, looking at this passage in light of contemporary scholars of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and similar texts, they maintain that the discrimination of the two natures—
the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the dependent (*paratantra*)— is called "unreal.
That the imagined nature is non-existent and the dependent nature is unarisen is termed the "perfected nature" (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
This accords with the meaning for those of inferior faculties.
If one regards the three natures as unreal,
then the principle of the three non-natures is called the reality.
Regarding the meaning of those of middling faculties,
since he does not state that they are neither of the three natures nor of the three non-natures, there is no sense of those of superior faculties therein;
however, according to the intention of Vasubandhu, such [a category] must indeed exist.
Yet, if a student does not receive the refined spirit of Nāgārjuna, they will lack even a single phrase of this profound essence.
This is called "The Dharmas of All Buddhas," which is the second summary of the four-line teaching’s intent.
If one enters into the principle of transcending the four through these four gates,
then these four are called the Buddha-dharma,
and they also serve as the four gates.
If one clings to these four propositions and, unable to realize the absence of the four through them, instead forms interpretations based on individual attachments,
then these four propositions are not the Buddha-dharma,
nor can they be called "gates."
Because they are unable to penetrate into the principle.
If that is so, then for the scholars of the four treatises who follow the tradition of Nāgārjuna, these four propositions are all skillful applications of the present time.
The former interpretation merely grasps one branch of the application of skillful means;

The first half of the second verse clarifies that time exists in dependence upon things.
Thus, phenomena constitute the substance of time.
The second half of the verse clarifies that because phenomena do not exist, time does not exist;
for example, one knows the seasons of spring and autumn through phenomena such as flowers and fruits.
Since things such as flowers and fruits have been variously analyzed above and found to be non-existent,
and because they are non-existent, time also does not exist.
Thus it is asked.
If temporal phenomena depend upon one another, why do they not mutually serve as each other's substance?
Furthermore, it was asked: "Since time has no separate substance, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) should be unable to take it as an object."
Furthermore, it should not be an object of the mental faculty (dharmāyatana),
yet because the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) takes it as its object, it is indeed obtained; thus,
it is also an object of the mental faculty.
It would, therefore, have to be a distinct entity.
If it lacked an entity, it would lack time.
Furthermore, if the present were dependent upon the future, they would necessarily exist in mutual relation.
If it cannot exist, it also cannot be depended upon.
*Madhyamaka-śāstra-vṛtti*, Scroll Eight, End.
